Brick
BRIK
noun
From the Old French brique, a fragment or lump, related to break; rendering the Hebrew lebenah, from laban, “to be white,” the pale mud block moulded and dried — man’s manufactured substitute for stone.

Biblical Definition

Brick is the first building material named in Scripture, and it is named at Babel. The men of Shinar said one to another, Go to, let us make brick, and burn them throughly — and the narrative adds the telling clause, they had brick for stone, and slime for morter. Brick is not what God gives; it is what man makes. Stone is quarried out of creation; brick is compounded of dust and fire in a kiln, uniform, mass-produced, fit for raising a tower whose top may reach unto heaven and for making a name. Set beside it the LORD’s own instruction for His altar: if thou wilt make me an altar of stone, thou shalt not build it of hewn stone, for if thou lift up thy tool upon it, thou hast polluted it (Exo 20:25). Unhewn stone for God’s altar; burnt brick for man’s tower. Then brick becomes the very substance of bondage: Israel’s lives were made bitter with hard bondage “in morter, and in brick” (Exo 1:14), and when Pharaoh withheld the straw the officers were beaten and cried, “There is no straw given unto thy servants, and they say to us, Make brick” (Exo 5:16). And at the end the same defiance returns: “The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones” (Isa 9:10) — a people under judgment answering God with a construction plan.

Webster 1828 Definition

A mass of clay moulded and hardened by fire or sun for building; in Scripture the material of Babel’s tower and of Israel’s bondage in Egypt.

expand to see more

BRICK, a mass of clay tempered with water, formed into a long square, and baked or burnt in a kiln.

From the French brique, a fragment or piece; allied to break.

Bricks are used for walls and buildings where stone is scarce or costly.

In Scripture, the material of the tower of Babel, brick being used for stone (Gen 11:3).

The forced labor of the Israelites in Egypt consisted in making brick (Exo 1:14; 5:16).

Key Scripture

Exo 1:14 — "And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field: all their service, wherein they made them serve, was with rigour."

Exo 5:16 — "There is no straw given unto thy servants, and they say to us, Make brick: and, behold, thy servants are beaten; but the fault is in thine own people."

Isa 9:10 — "The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones: the sycomores are cut down, but we will change them into cedars."

Isa 65:3 — "A people that provoketh me to anger continually to my face; that sacrificeth in gardens, and burneth incense upon altars of brick;"

Modern Corruption

Babel is retold as a fable about diversity or as a myth explaining languages, and its actual sin — a manufactured ascent to heaven undertaken to make man a name — is exactly the project the modern West is still running.

expand to see more

Two misreadings compete. The first treats Gen 11 as legendary material, an etiological tale invented to explain why men speak different tongues; the second, common in pulpits, reduces it to a lesson about pride in general with no reference to the specific thing the builders wanted. Both miss the text. The builders state their own aim twice: let us build us a city and a tower whose top may reach unto heaven, and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered. It is a religious project and a political one at once — a way up to God of human manufacture, and a unity of mankind secured by concentration rather than by covenant. The brick is not incidental to it. Brick is the technology that made the tower possible: standardized, kiln-hardened, requiring no quarry, no mountain, no gift of God, only clay and fire and organized labour. Man’s religion has always preferred brick, because brick can be made to specification and stone must be received.

Recover the contrast God Himself draws, for it runs from Genesis to the cross. At Babel man builds upward with burnt brick to reach heaven and make a name; at Sinai God forbids a tool to be lifted on the stone of His altar, lest the worshipper contribute anything to the place where blood is shed for him. Every altar of brick is a work of man’s hands, which is why Isaiah lists them among the provocations of an apostate people (Isa 65:3). The gospel is the end of brickmaking. There is a stone the builders rejected which is become the head of the corner; believers are lively stones built up a spiritual house, not bricks pressed from one mould; and the name man could not make for himself at Shinar God gives freely in Christ, a new name written, to them that overcome. And the bondage of Exo 1:14 tells us where the brickyard ends: the man who insists on building his own way to heaven finishes as a slave in the morter, beaten for a quota he can never fill.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew lebenah, from laban, to be white — the pale sun-dried or kiln-burnt block; contrasted throughout Scripture with 'eben, stone, which is found rather than made.

expand to see more

Hebrew — lebenah (לבנה), a brick, from laban (לבן), to be white; the pale clay block of Mesopotamia and Egypt.

Hebrew — 'eben (אבן), stone, quarried and given; the material God requires for His altar, unhewn (Exo 20:25).

Hebrew — chemar (חמר), bitumen or slime, the mortar of Babel, distinguished from lime morter.

Greek (LXX) — plinthos (πλίνθος), a brick or tile; whence the English plinth.

Sense — the whole theology of the word lies in one clause of Gen 11:3: they had brick for stone.

Usage

"“They had brick for stone — and that clause is the history of every man-made religion since.”"

"“Unhewn stone for God’s altar, burnt brick for man’s tower; the two builders are never confused in Scripture.”"

"“Israel’s lives were made bitter in morter and in brick, and the quota never once came down.”"
